cases.title: The disappearing margin
cases.summary: Sales are steady. Profits are not. Find the change that matters.
cases.brief: Aruna Cement sells 1 million tonnes a year. Annual operating profit fell from ₹100 crore to ₹60 crore. The CEO wants to recover the lost ₹40 crore within 12 months, without major capital expenditure. Diagnose the decline and recommend the next move. All case data is fictional.
objective: Maximise market share at any cost

exhibits.title: Revenue & cost bridge
exhibits.text: Annual volume: 1 million tonnes in both years. Realisation: ₹5,000/t in both years. Fuel: ₹800 → ₹1,100/t. Power: ₹400 → ₹500/t. Other operating costs: ₹2,800/t, unchanged.

exhibits.title: Plant performance
exhibits.text: Throughput and product quality are stable. Fuel consumption per tonne is unchanged; delivered fuel price rose 37.5%. Electricity consumption per tonne is unchanged; tariff rose 25%.

exhibits.title: Available interventions
exhibits.text: An alternative fuel blend could save ₹200/t across annual output, before a one-time ₹2 crore trial cost. Quality and throughput effects are untested. A power contract could save ₹50/t. Both can operate within 12 months; no other quantified savings are available.

exhibits.title: Market & customers
exhibits.text: Market size, share and customer mix are stable. Competitors have spare capacity. Customers are price-sensitive; no price increase has been validated.

exhibits.title: Supplier landscape
exhibits.text: Existing fuel suppliers can offer shorter contracts but have not quoted a reduction. Alternative fuel availability and delivered quality must be verified; lower price alone does not prove lower cost per tonne of cement.

exhibits.title: Customer economics
exhibits.text: The sales team has proposed targeted pricing, but customer loss and contribution impact need testing. No blanket price increase is yet established.

calc.question: How much of the annual profit decline is explained by the fuel cost increase? Enter ₹ crore.
calc.hint: Convert rupees into crore: ₹1 crore = ₹10 million.

hypothesis: Energy input prices explain the entire ₹40 crore decline
Lower utilisation is the main cause
Falling selling prices explain the decline
cases.hypothesisFeedback: Fuel contributes ₹30 crore and power ₹10 crore. Consumption intensity is unchanged, so the evidence points to prices, not process efficiency.
decision: Pilot the fuel blend and validate the power contract; acknowledge the remaining gap
Immediately switch all fuel and promise full ₹40 crore recovery
Increase production to solve the margin decline
cases.decisionFeedback: Fuel saves ₹20 crore and power ₹5 crore annually. After the ₹2 crore trial, first-year savings are ₹23 crore: a ₹17 crore gap remains. Validate quality and throughput before scaling.
cases.model: The full ₹40 crore decline is explained by fuel and power prices. Pilot the fuel blend with quality and throughput guardrails and validate the power contract. The quantified package delivers ₹23 crore in the first year, leaving ₹17 crore to address through further cost and pricing work. Assign owners and review trial results before rollout.
cases.drill: Practise converting per-tonne changes into annual profit impact, then separate recurring savings from one-time costs.

cases.title: A new city, a real decision
cases.summary: A promising market is only the beginning. Should a meal brand enter Pune?
cases.brief: FreshTable is considering a Pune launch of its meal subscription service. The board requires at least ₹1 crore annual operating profit at steady state and a credible acquisition plan. Recommend whether to proceed. Ignore tax, financing and working capital. All case data is fictional.
objective: Assess profit potential and validate demand before scaling

exhibits.title: Demand & reachable customers
exhibits.text: There are 100,000 target households. Research suggests 8% may subscribe, but this is stated intent, not paid conversion. Base plan assumes 5,000 subscribers. Each orders 20 meals/month for 12 months.

exhibits.title: Unit economics
exhibits.text: Price: ₹150/meal. Food, delivery and packaging: ₹110/meal. Annual fixed operating costs: ₹3 crore. These costs exclude first-time customer acquisition.

exhibits.title: Acquisition & retention
exhibits.text: Estimated initial acquisition cost: ₹2,000/subscriber. For this exercise, assume the initial subscribers stay for a full year. Real retention and acquisition costs are unvalidated. A limited paid pilot is feasible.

exhibits.title: Competitive context
exhibits.text: Three competitors serve the city. Interviews suggest consistency and reliable delivery matter more than menu variety. No willingness-to-pay study has yet been run.

exhibits.title: Customer occasions
exhibits.text: Office clusters offer dense routes but weekday concentration. Residential subscribers may be more dispersed. The 5,000-subscriber base case has not been allocated between these groups.

exhibits.title: Operating constraints
exhibits.text: Delivery reliability and food consistency must be maintained. No ability to serve more than 5,000 customers at the current cost is assumed without validation.

calc.question: At 5,000 subscribers, what is annual operating profit before acquisition costs? Enter ₹ crore.
calc.hint: Calculate contribution per meal, then annual meals, then subtract fixed costs.

hypothesis: The full target market will subscribe
The base case clears the steady-state target, but demand and retention need validation
cases.hypothesisFeedback: ₹1.8 crore steady-state operating profit exceeds the ₹1 crore hurdle. But the assumed subscriber base and retention have not been validated.
decision: Launch at full scale based on survey intent
Run a paid pilot, validate retention and acquisition, then decide on scale
cases.decisionFeedback: Initial acquisition costs are ₹1 crore at 5,000 subscribers, reducing first-year profit to ₹0.8 crore under the exercise assumptions. Distinguish that from the ₹1.8 crore steady-state figure.
cases.model: The base case produces ₹1.8 crore annual operating profit before acquisition, above the steady-state hurdle. First-year profit is ₹0.8 crore after initial acquisition. Recommend a paid pilot to measure conversion, retention, delivery reliability and acquisition cost before committing to a full launch.
cases.drill: Build a three-line sensitivity analysis for subscriber count, contribution per meal and retention.

cases.title: The capacity illusion
cases.summary: Demand is waiting. Identify the bottleneck before buying equipment.
cases.brief: A packaged-food factory needs to supply 48,000 packs/day. It currently makes 40,000. The COO proposes a new filling line. Recommend a way to close the gap with minimal investment. Assume an 8-hour day, sufficient materials and no inventory buffers between stages. All case data is fictional.
objective: Increase filling capacity regardless of other stages
Meet demand by addressing the system constraint
Maximise the speed of every machine

exhibits.title: Line capacity
exhibits.text: Effective capacities: mixing 7,000 packs/hour; filling 8,000; packing 5,000. Current output is 40,000 packs/day over 8 hours. These effective rates already include current losses.

exhibits.title: Packing losses
exhibits.text: Packing nameplate rate is 7,000/hour. Its current effective rate is 5,000/hour due to changeovers and minor stops. A trial suggests 6,200/hour may be feasible with standardised setups and maintenance.

exhibits.title: Improvement choices
exhibits.text: A new filling line costs ₹1 crore and increases filling capacity to 12,000/hour. Packing improvements cost ₹8 lakh and could raise its effective capacity to 6,200/hour, subject to sustained trial results.

exhibits.title: Quality & demand
exhibits.text: Demand is 48,000/day for the next six months. Rejects are already reflected in effective capacities. Faster packing must retain seal quality. No demand above 48,000/day is confirmed.

exhibits.title: Product mix
exhibits.text: Demand varies across product formats. The current average rate does not prove capability for every shift and format.

exhibits.title: Rate measurement
exhibits.text: Use good packs after rejects when measuring effective rate. Avoid deducting the same loss twice.

calc.question: If packing sustains 6,200 packs/hour, what is the maximum daily line output over 8 hours?
calc.hint: The slowest effective stage limits the whole line. Do not subtract losses again.

hypothesis: Filling is the constraint because it has the proposed investment
Packing constrains the line; improving filling alone does not increase output
Mixing is already too slow for demand
cases.hypothesisFeedback: Packing limits output to 5,000/hour × 8 = 40,000/day. A faster filling line would still wait for packing.
decision: Buy the new filling line immediately
Trial packing improvements, verify quality and sustain at least 6,000/hour
cases.decisionFeedback: 6,000/hour meets demand; 6,200 provides only a 3.3% capacity cushion. Validate performance across shifts and product mixes before promising reliable supply.
cases.model: Packing is the constraint. Trial the ₹8 lakh setup and maintenance improvements rather than the ₹1 crore filling investment. At 6,200/hour the line could supply 49,600/day, enough for current demand with a small cushion. Verify seal quality and sustained performance across shifts.
cases.drill: Practise identifying the minimum effective capacity, and distinguish theoretical capacity from reliable daily delivery.

cases.title: The discount dilemma
cases.summary: More customers or higher contribution? Evaluate a pricing change and a segmented alternative.
cases.brief: LedgerNest sells subscription software to small businesses. It has 10,000 customers paying ₹1,000/month. The CEO wants to improve next-year operating profit by at least ₹1 crore without reducing service quality. Sales proposes a 15% price cut. Advise the CEO. All figures are fictional; ignore tax, financing and working capital.
objective: Improve annual operating profit by ₹1 crore while maintaining service quality

exhibits.title: Current economics
exhibits.text: 10,000 customers; price ₹1,000/customer/month; variable service cost ₹300/customer/month; annual fixed costs ₹5 crore. All customer counts in the base plan are full-year averages.

exhibits.title: Sales proposal
exhibits.text: A 15% price cut is projected to lift full-year average customers by 25%. Variable cost remains ₹300/customer/month. Fixed cost does not change. No paid experiment validates this projection.

exhibits.title: Customer segments
exhibits.text: 7,000 standard users and 3,000 advanced users currently pay the same price. Advanced users ask for audit logs and integrations. Willingness to pay is untested.

exhibits.title: Service capacity
exhibits.text: The current support team can serve up to 13,000 customers at the stated cost and quality. Above that, additional staffing would be needed; its cost is not yet estimated.

exhibits.title: Experiment design
exhibits.text: A test needs a control group, customer-level contribution, support effort and churn tracking. A short promotional response is not proof of a durable uplift.

calc.question: What is current annual operating profit? Enter ₹ crore.
calc.hint: Use contribution, not revenue.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: The baseline contribution is ₹8.4 crore and operating profit ₹3.4 crore. A price reduction must generate enough additional contribution to offset the lower margin.
cases.decisionFeedback: A defensible decision compares customer response, contribution, service capacity and evidence quality, rather than revenue growth alone.
cases.model: Do not approve a broad price cut on an unvalidated volume projection. Test a segmented premium offer or a limited discount experiment, compare contribution and retention, and protect service quality.
cases.drill: Calculate the customer increase needed to offset a price cut, then test whether support capacity can handle it.

cases.title: The warehouse promise
cases.summary: A regional hub promises lower costs. Test freight savings, inventory and execution risk.
cases.brief: RouteWorks distributes industrial spares from Chennai to southern India. Annual delivery cost is rising and customers complain about late orders. The COO proposes a Bengaluru hub. Find a way to improve service while saving at least ₹20 lakh/year after recurring costs. One-time setup must pay back within two years. All data is fictional. Ignore tax and financing; treat inventory carrying cost as a recurring operating cost.
objective: Improve service and save ₹20 lakh/year with setup payback within two years

exhibits.title: Demand by region
exhibits.text: Annual shipments: Tamil Nadu 60,000; Karnataka 30,000; Kerala 10,000. Customer demand is stable. All figures are shipments, not tonnes.

exhibits.title: Current shipping cost
exhibits.text: Current delivered cost/shipment: Tamil Nadu ₹120; Karnataka ₹300; Kerala ₹250. These include line haul and local delivery. Other costs are unchanged unless specified.

exhibits.title: Service performance
exhibits.text: On-time rates: Tamil Nadu 95%, Karnataka 78%, Kerala 85%. Of Karnataka late orders, 60% involve carrier transit and 40% involve late warehouse release. Do not assume all late orders have one cause.

exhibits.title: Available paths
exhibits.text: A Karnataka hub changes the freight network and stocks inventory locally. A carrier-and-cutoff programme keeps the current network. Both require detailed economics and a service pilot.

exhibits.title: Order release
exhibits.text: Late release sometimes comes from inaccurate stock records and approval holds. A carrier contract alone will not remove those delays.

calc.question: What is the current annual shipping cost across all three regions? Enter ₹ lakh.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: Karnataka has the weakest service and the highest cost per shipment, but both transport and warehouse release contribute to lateness.
cases.decisionFeedback: Separate freight savings, fixed site costs, inventory carrying costs and one-time setup. A cheaper shipment is not necessarily a cheaper network.
cases.model: Compare a Karnataka hub with a carrier-and-release pilot. Require evidence that the proposed operating model improves both economics and on-time delivery. Include inventory and transition costs.
cases.drill: Build a total-cost bridge and state the conditions under which a regional hub beats a process improvement.

cases.title: Seats are not outcomes
cases.summary: An education programme must choose whom to reach and how to measure learning.
cases.brief: An education foundation has ₹60 lakh for a one-year programme covering up to 20,000 eligible students. It wants at least 3,000 additional students to achieve a defined mastery threshold relative to no programme. Recommend an approach that addresses both learning and access. All numbers are fictional planning assumptions; this is a programme-design case, not a claim about any teaching method.
objective: Generate at least 3,000 additional mastery outcomes within ₹60 lakh, considering access

exhibits.title: Baseline and eligibility
exhibits.text: 20,000 eligible students; 40% are expected to meet the mastery threshold without the programme. There are no fees paid by students. The target concerns additional mastery outcomes, not enrolment.

exhibits.title: Digital programme
exhibits.text: Digital programme budget: ₹12 lakh fixed + ₹600/enrolled student. Enrol 8,000 students in the base plan. An assumed 80% engage consistently. Engaged students are assumed to have a 30 percentage-point mastery uplift versus their no-programme outcome; non-engaged students have zero uplift.

exhibits.title: Access constraints
exhibits.text: 60% of eligible students have reliable digital access. Students without access are not assumed equivalent in learning needs or support. No transport or device programme is included in the initial budget.

exhibits.title: Evidence quality
exhibits.text: The uplift estimates come from a small voluntary pilot without random assignment. Selection bias, attrition and differences in prior attainment are unresolved. Treat estimates as scenarios, not causal proof.

exhibits.title: Measurement plan
exhibits.text: Use a common pre/post assessment and comparison group; track attendance, attrition and outcomes by access group. Discuss fair allocation and informed participation with programme leaders.

calc.question: At 8,000 digital enrolments, what is the expected number of additional mastery outcomes under the stated assumptions?
calc.working: 8,000 × 80% × 30 percentage points = 1,920 additional mastery outcomes.
calc.hint: Use absolute uplift, not a 30% relative increase.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: The base digital programme costs ₹60 lakh but produces only 1,920 expected additional outcomes. Spending the full budget is not the same as achieving the objective.
cases.decisionFeedback: Compare reach, engagement, uplift, cost and access. An honest recommendation may acknowledge that the target is not feasible under the tested assumptions.
cases.model: Do not promise 3,000 additional outcomes based on the small pilot. Compare programme designs, estimate the target gap and conduct a staged evaluation that addresses access and selection bias.
cases.drill: Separate reach, engagement, percentage-point uplift and causal evidence in a programme impact calculation.

cases.title: How many cups?
cases.summary: Estimate a city’s takeaway coffee demand, defend your assumptions and cross-check from the supply side.
cases.brief: Estimate the number of paid takeaway coffee cups sold on a typical weekday within Chennai municipal limits. Include delivery and street vendors; exclude home-made coffee and dine-in cups. Estimate cups, not unique customers or revenue. Build your own assumptions without looking up the answer, give a range and explain how you would validate it. This is a fictional estimation exercise: all later numerical anchors are hypothetical, not facts about Chennai.
objective: Produce an assumption-led weekday cup estimate and a defensible range; no business recommendation is required.

exhibits.title: Market boundary
exhibits.text: Count a delivered cup once, at the seller. A buyer can purchase multiple cups. Keep the geographic boundary and typical weekday consistent across methods.

exhibits.title: Demand-side structure
exhibits.text: A possible decomposition is residents × relevant age share × daily outside-coffee buying share × takeaway share × cups per buyer. You may propose a different mutually exclusive segmentation. Choose and explain your own initial values.

exhibits.title: Supply-side structure
exhibits.text: A cross-check can use number of sellers × daily takeaway cups per seller, segmented by shop type. Watch for overlapping directories, peak-hour bias and delivery already included in seller counts.

exhibits.title: Uncertainty and data needs
exhibits.text: Population boundary, purchase frequency, takeaway share, seller counts and seller throughput may all be uncertain. Identify which assumptions dominate the result; distinguish a plausible scenario range from a statistical confidence interval.

calc.question: Enter your own first estimate of takeaway cups per weekday. Explain the assumptions and a plausible low–high range below.
calc.working: There is no fixed correct total here. Review the boundary, decomposition, arithmetic under your own assumptions, plausible range and independent cross-check. Later numerical exercises check arithmetic under explicitly supplied hypothetical inputs.
calc.hint: Start with either people and purchase frequency or sellers and daily throughput. State what each factor includes.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: A useful estimate makes assumptions visible and keeps people, purchases and cups distinct. An order-of-magnitude answer without a derivation is difficult to assess.
cases.decisionFeedback: Defend a range, triangulate with an independent method and name the highest-value data to obtain. A different well-supported initial number is not automatically wrong.
cases.model: Give your own estimate with its derivation and uncertainty. Under the later hypothetical inputs, demand- and supply-side results are of similar order, but neither is a verified market fact.
cases.drill: Re-estimate the market using a different decomposition, then change the two assumptions with the greatest influence.

cases.title: What actually went wrong?
cases.summary: Orders appear to have fallen. Separate the real problem from measurement errors before suggesting fixes.
cases.brief: CartLane’s dashboard shows completed weekly orders falling from 50,000 to 40,000 after a new app release. Leadership suspects delivery capacity and wants to buy more capacity. Your assignment is ONLY to identify and define the problem: establish what changed, where it is concentrated, which explanations remain plausible and what evidence would distinguish them. Do not propose a solution or an implementation plan. Two comparable weeks are used; all figures are fictional.
objective: Produce a quantified problem statement with evidence, uncertainty and a focused verification plan; do not choose an intervention.

exhibits.title: Headline performance
exhibits.text: Recorded completed orders: previous week 50,000; current week 40,000. Checkout attempts: 100,000 in each week. The dashboard definition of completed order is unchanged, but that does not establish that data capture is unchanged.

exhibits.title: Recorded funnel
exhibits.text: App-recorded successful payment confirmations: 80,000 → 64,000. App-recorded completed orders: 50,000 → 40,000. Thus recorded completion per recorded payment confirmation is unchanged. These are app records, not independent bank or shipment reconciliations.

exhibits.title: Platform split
exhibits.text: Android: 60,000 checkout attempts in each week; app-recorded payment confirmations 48,000 → 32,000. iOS: 40,000 attempts in each week; confirmations 32,000 in each week. The release was Android-only.

exhibits.title: Delivery operations
exhibits.text: Available delivery slots and carrier staffing are unchanged. Sample on-time performance is stable. These observations weaken the capacity hypothesis but cannot prove capacity is irrelevant for every segment.

exhibits.title: Timeline and comparability
exhibits.text: The app release and a campaign happened in the same week. Traffic volume is unchanged, but customer mix may differ. No randomised rollout or controlled experiment has been run. Temporal association alone is not causal proof.

calc.question: What is the percentage decline in RECORDED completed orders?
calc.working: (50,000 − 40,000)/50,000 × 100 = 20%. This describes a recorded decline, not yet a verified operational decline.
calc.hint: Use the previous week as the denominator.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: The recorded loss appears upstream of fulfilment, in Android payment confirmation. Unchanged recorded downstream conversion weakens a simple delivery-capacity story, but independent measurement is needed.
cases.decisionFeedback: The deliverable is a bounded diagnosis, not a fix. Distinguish symptoms, measurement artefacts, candidate mechanisms and a proven root cause.
cases.model: The dashboard shows a 20% order decline, with a recorded payment-confirmation loss concentrated on Android. Do not label this a delivery-capacity problem or an app defect without reconciliation and causal evidence.
cases.drill: Write a problem statement with affected segment, magnitude, timing, evidence and remaining uncertainty—without including a proposed solution.

cases.title: Build it or partner?
cases.summary: Compare ownership and partnership using cash flows, downside risk and service constraints.
cases.brief: ColdLink is considering a five-year temperature-controlled storage service. It can build its own facility or use a specialist partner. Expected annual volume is 70,000 pallet-months. The board wants positive net present value at a 10% discount rate and evidence that 98% on-time availability can be sustained. Recommend whether and how to proceed. All figures are fictional. Ignore tax, financing, working capital and residual value; annual operating cash flows occur at year-end. The five-year annuity factor at 10% is supplied as 3.791.
objective: Compare risk-adjusted investment attractiveness and service feasibility; do not equate accounting profit or payback with NPV.

exhibits.title: Demand and scope
exhibits.text: Base demand: 70,000 pallet-months/year for five years. A pallet stored for one month is one pallet-month. Demand is a forecast, not signed contracts. Both options have capacity for the base case.

exhibits.title: Owned facility economics
exhibits.text: Upfront investment ₹200 lakh at time zero. Price ₹200/pallet-month; variable operating cost ₹80/pallet-month; annual fixed cash cost ₹24 lakh. No other recurring or terminal cash flows are assumed.

exhibits.title: Partner economics
exhibits.text: Upfront integration cost ₹20 lakh. Net contribution after all partner variable charges is ₹60/pallet-month. Annual contract-management cash cost ₹8 lakh. No other recurring or terminal cash flows are assumed.

exhibits.title: Valuation convention
exhibits.text: For a constant annual cash flow over five years, present value equals annual cash flow × 3.791. NPV equals that present value minus time-zero investment. Use the supplied rounded factor consistently.

exhibits.title: Strategic and service considerations
exhibits.text: The owned facility offers more process control but demands operating capability. The partner reduces capital commitment but introduces dependence, audit and exit risks. Neither option has yet demonstrated the 98% service target for this customer mix.

calc.question: Calculate annual operating CASH FLOW for the owned facility at base demand. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.working: 70,000×(₹200−₹80)/100,000 − ₹24 lakh = ₹60 lakh/year, before time-zero investment.
calc.hint: Contribution less fixed cash costs; do not deduct the capital outlay annually.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: The owned facility generates positive annual cash flow, but the investment decision also requires capital timing, alternative economics and service feasibility.
cases.decisionFeedback: Compare NPV under consistent assumptions, test downside scenarios and consider control, dependence and reversibility. A positive NPV does not establish service feasibility.
cases.model: Both base options have positive NPV under the supplied assumptions, with the partner requiring less upfront capital. A defensible decision tests demand, service and contract risks before committing; it may favour a conditional partnership rather than an unconditional launch.
cases.drill: Compare two investments with different capital requirements using consistent cash-flow timing, then test what could invalidate the preferred option.

cases.title: Where did the orders go?
cases.summary: Orders fell 13% in a week. Find where in the funnel, for whom, and what to do now.
cases.brief: BasketNow is a 20-minute grocery delivery app in five cities. Weekly orders fell from 4,00,000 to 3,47,500 in the week starting 3 March, about 13% down on the week before. Leadership wants to know what happened, how sure you are, and what to do this week. All data is fictional.
objective: Explain the order drop with a clear confidence level and recommend an action for this week.

exhibits.title: Weekly orders trend
exhibits.text: Weekly orders in the three weeks before 3 March: 4,02,000; 3,98,000; 4,00,000. Week starting 3 March: 3,47,500. The same week last year was 1% up on the week before. An order is counted when payment succeeds.

exhibits.title: Funnel, prior week vs latest week
exhibits.text: App sessions: 20,00,000 → 20,00,000. Sessions with an item added to cart: 8,00,000 → 8,00,000. Checkouts started: 5,00,000 → 5,00,000. Payments succeeded: 4,00,000 → 3,47,500.

exhibits.title: Platforms and releases
exhibits.text: Android carries 70% of checkouts and iOS 30%, in both weeks. Android app version 8.2 was released to half of Android users on 3 March. It moved payment to a new in-app checkout page and added a saved-UPI option. It passed QA on test devices.

exhibits.title: Market and pricing
exhibits.text: No competitor launches, price changes or delivery-fee changes in the period. Marketing spend was unchanged. Weather and holidays were normal in all five cities.

exhibits.title: City split
exhibits.text: Each of the five cities shows orders down between 12% and 14%. Sessions in every city are within 1% of the prior week.

calc.question: Payment success is payments succeeded ÷ checkouts started. By how many percentage points did it fall between the prior week and the latest week?
calc.working: Prior week: 4,00,000 ÷ 5,00,000 = 80%. Latest week: 3,47,500 ÷ 5,00,000 = 69.5%. Fall: 80 − 69.5 = 10.5 percentage points. Every earlier funnel step is flat, so the whole drop sits at payment.
calc.hint: Work out the conversion rate for each week, then subtract. A change in a rate is measured in percentage points.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: Sessions, carts and checkouts are flat, so demand has not changed. The whole drop is at the payment step, which points to the payment flow rather than the market.
cases.decisionFeedback: Act on what is established, such as pausing or rolling back the release for affected users, while verifying the exact cause. Measure recovery against users who were never affected.
cases.model: Demand is unchanged: the drop sits at payment success, which fell from 80% to 69.5% when Android 8.2 shipped. Pause or roll back the release now, verify the exact cause, and confirm that orders recover to about 4,00,000 a week.
cases.drill: Practise funnel maths: work out step-by-step conversion for two periods and find the step where the change happens.

cases.title: Did the streak work?
cases.summary: A streak feature lifted retention in an A/B test. Decide whether it really helps learners and the business.
cases.brief: PadhoPlus is a vocabulary-learning app with a 14-day free trial, then a paid subscription. It ran an A/B test of a daily streak: a counter showing how many days in a row a learner has practised, plus a 9 pm reminder. Leadership wants to know whether to launch it to everyone. They care about learning and paid subscribers, not just app opens. All data is fictional.
objective: Decide whether to launch the streak, using a primary metric chosen in advance plus guardrails for learning quality and revenue.

exhibits.title: Experiment design
exhibits.text: New sign-ups over four weeks were split at random, 50/50. Control: 40,000 learners. Streak: 40,000 learners. The primary metric, written down before the test, is week-4 retention: the share of learners active in their fourth week.

exhibits.title: Topline results
exhibits.text: Week-1 retention: control 30%, streak 36%. Week-4 retention: control 18.0%, streak 19.8%. Lessons completed per active learner per week: control 12, streak 11. The data team says the week-4 difference is statistically significant.

exhibits.title: Learning quality
exhibits.text: Average score on review quizzes: control 72%, streak 64%. Streak learners did more of the shortest 1-minute quick-review lessons, which keep a streak alive.

exhibits.title: Notifications
exhibits.text: Streak learners got a 9 pm reminder if they had not practised that day. Turned off notifications by week 4: control 2%, streak 5%.

exhibits.title: Business goal
exhibits.text: The goal this year is more paid subscribers. Retention is used as a leading indicator because most learners who pay are still active at the end of their trial.

calc.question: What is the relative lift in week-4 retention for the streak group compared with control? Enter %.
calc.working: (19.8% − 18.0%) ÷ 18.0% = 1.8 ÷ 18 = 10% relative lift. In absolute terms that is 1.8 percentage points.
calc.hint: Relative lift is the difference divided by the control rate. Do not confuse it with the 1.8-point absolute difference.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: The streak lifts early retention, but shorter lessons, lower quiz scores and more notification opt-outs suggest it may reward opening the app rather than learning.
cases.decisionFeedback: Weigh the primary metric against the guardrails. Launching, redesigning or testing further can all be defensible if tied to the evidence.
cases.model: Week-4 retention rose 10% in relative terms (18.0% to 19.8%), but lessons per learner and quiz scores fell. A defensible answer holds the launch and tests a streak that rewards full lessons, with learning-quality guardrails.
cases.drill: Practise relative versus absolute change: convert retention rates into percentage-point and percentage lifts, then into numbers of users.

cases.title: Which feature first?
cases.summary: Three feature ideas, one quarter. Choose what to build for small shopkeepers and how to test it.
cases.brief: KiranaPay is a UPI payments app used by 2 lakh kirana shopkeepers to accept payments. The team can build one major feature this quarter. Three ideas are on the table: instant settlement of payments to the bank, a simple stock tracker, and small working-capital loans through a lending partner. Recommend which to build first and how to test it. All data is fictional.
objective: Choose the one feature to build first, based on the most important user problem, the size of the opportunity and the effort, and plan how to test it.

exhibits.title: Shopkeeper segments
exhibits.text: 2,00,000 active shopkeepers. Small stores (under ₹5,000 of UPI sales a day): 1,40,000, averaging ₹2,000 a day. Larger stores: 60,000, averaging ₹10,000 a day, so they carry about 68% of payment value. Monthly churn: small stores 4%, larger stores 2%.

exhibits.title: User research
exhibits.text: Interviews with 40 shopkeepers. Waiting until the next day for money to reach the bank: raised by 26, mostly larger stores that pay suppliers the same day. Needing ₹20,000–₹50,000 for festival stock: raised by 18, mostly larger stores. Running out of fast-moving stock: raised by 14, mostly small stores.

exhibits.title: The three ideas
exhibits.text: Instant settlement: money reaches the bank within minutes, for a 0.3% fee on the value settled. Stock tracker: record sales by item and get low-stock alerts; free. Working-capital loans: average ₹25,000 through a lending partner; KiranaPay earns 2% of the amount lent.

exhibits.title: Engineering estimates
exhibits.text: Instant settlement: 2 months, because the bank partner already supports it. Stock tracker: 4 months, because it needs an item catalogue and a new app section. Loans: 5 months, including partner integration, risk checks and regulatory review.

exhibits.title: Competitors
exhibits.text: Two rival apps settle the next day for free. One offers loans to larger stores. None has a stock tracker.

calc.question: Larger stores average ₹10,000 of UPI sales a day. If 30% of them adopt instant settlement and settle all their sales instantly, what monthly fee revenue does it earn? Assume 30 days. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.working: 60,000 × 30% = 18,000 stores. 18,000 × ₹10,000 × 30 days = ₹540 crore settled a month. 0.3% of ₹540 crore = ₹1.62 crore = ₹162 lakh a month.
calc.hint: Stores × sales per day × days gives the value settled; then apply the 0.3% fee. ₹1 crore = ₹100 lakh.

cases.hypothesisFeedback: The most common problem in the research is slow settlement for larger stores, who carry about two-thirds of payment value. The stock tracker addresses a real but less frequent problem, mostly for small stores.
cases.decisionFeedback: Choose one feature and say what you are giving up. Test it with a small first version, a success metric and a condition for stopping.
cases.model: Instant settlement solves the most raised problem for the stores that carry about two-thirds of payment value, earns fee revenue (about ₹162 lakh a month at 30% adoption) and is the quickest to build. Build it first and pilot it with a group of larger stores.
cases.drill: Practise prioritisation maths: work out RICE scores and simple revenue estimates for two or three options, then find which input changes the ranking.

clarifications: What counts as success?
Recover the ₹40 crore profit decline; management will consider a partial recovery if the remaining gap is explicit. Do not assume volume growth.
Can we invest?
Major capacity investment is out of scope. Trials and changes in procurement or commercial terms are possible.
How should first-year savings be treated?
Use full-year implementation only when specified. Later scenarios change availability or volume and replace the relevant original assumptions.

extra.title: Supplier landscape
extra.text: Existing fuel suppliers can offer shorter contracts but have not quoted a reduction. Alternative fuel availability and delivered quality must be verified; lower price alone does not prove lower cost per tonne of cement.

extra.title: Customer economics
extra.text: The sales team has proposed targeted pricing, but customer loss and contribution impact need testing. No blanket price increase is yet established.

branches.title: Fuel and procurement
branches.focus: Test fuel substitution and implementation timing.
branches.evidence: Full-year implementation case: alternative fuel saves ₹200 per tonne across 1 million tonnes. Power saves ₹50/t. One-time fuel trial costs ₹2 crore. Assume no volume or quality loss in this initial calculation.
branches.question: What does this package achieve in year one, and what still needs to be solved?

calc.question: Calculate total first-year savings for this package. Enter ₹ crore.
calc.working: Fuel ₹20 crore + power ₹5 crore − trial ₹2 crore = ₹23 crore. Recovery gap: ₹17 crore.
calc.hint: Separate recurring savings and trial cost.

branches.shock: New supplier evidence: the alternative fuel can cover only 60% of annual output in year one. Its ₹200/t saving applies only to that share. Power saving still applies to all output, and trial cost remains ₹2 crore. Quality performance is still unproven.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate first-year savings with 60% fuel coverage. Enter ₹ crore.
stressCalc.working: 0.6m tonnes×₹200 + 1m×₹50 − ₹2 crore = ₹15 crore. Gap: ₹25 crore.
stressCalc.hint: Only the fuel saving changes.

branches.probe: What trial measures and stop conditions would protect output and quality?
branches.model: A staged fuel trial plus power contract can deliver ₹15 crore under the updated availability constraint. Do not promise full recovery. Require delivered-quality checks, quality and throughput limits, and a supplier contingency.

branches.title: Customer and pricing
branches.focus: Test whether targeted pricing creates profit after volume loss.
branches.evidence: For this branch only, management can test a ₹150/t price increase on 400,000 tonnes of customer demand. It expects to lose 5% of this segment volume. At the original price, contribution on any lost tonne is ₹1,000. Other customer volumes and fixed costs stay unchanged. Ignore the fuel/power initiatives for this incremental pricing calculation.
branches.question: How would you assess the price proposal and distinguish revenue from profit impact?

calc.question: What is the incremental annual operating profit from the proposed price increase? Enter ₹ crore.
calc.working: Retained volume 380,000×₹150 = ₹5.7 crore; lost contribution 20,000×₹1,000 = ₹2 crore; net ₹3.7 crore.
calc.hint: Apply the price increase to retained tonnes and subtract lost contribution.

branches.shock: The customer pilot suggests volume loss of 12%, rather than 5%, in the targeted segment. The price increase and original contribution per tonne remain unchanged.

stressCalc.question: What is incremental annual profit with 12% volume loss? Enter ₹ crore.
stressCalc.hint: Revenue uplift and lost contribution have different bases.

branches.probe: What customer-level evidence would change your recommendation?
branches.model: Targeted pricing is positive at 12% volume loss, but only ₹0.48 crore. Break-even loss is about 13.04%; use a reversible, segmented test and do not treat it as a substitute for the energy-cost programme.

strong: Reconciles the full ₹40 crore decline and distinguishes input price from consumption efficiency.
States which assumptions changed and recalculates rather than repeating the first recommendation.
Makes the recovery gap explicit and defines quality, throughput and commercial guardrails.
pitfalls: Treating all energy inflation as an efficiency problem.
Counting recurring savings as first-year savings without testing coverage.
Calculating price impact on customers who leave.

clarifications: What is the profit hurdle?
At least ₹1 crore annual steady-state operating profit. First-year acquisition and cash requirements must also be discussed.
Is 8% intent equivalent to conversion?
No. It is a survey response, not a purchase commitment.
How do we handle retention?
The initial calculation assumes a full year. A later retention scenario explicitly replaces that simplifying assumption.

extra.title: Customer occasions
extra.text: Office clusters offer dense routes but weekday concentration. Residential subscribers may be more dispersed. The 5,000-subscriber base case has not been allocated between these groups.

extra.title: Operating constraints
extra.text: Delivery reliability and food consistency must be maintained. No ability to serve more than 5,000 customers at the current cost is assumed without validation.

branches.title: Acquisition and retention
branches.focus: Stress-test first-year economics against customer churn.
branches.evidence: Initial cohort: 5,000 subscribers, 20 meals/month, contribution ₹40/meal, annual fixed costs ₹3 crore. Initial acquisition cost is ₹2,000 per subscriber. All stay 12 months for this first calculation. No replacement acquisition is included.
branches.question: What could make a profitable steady-state plan unattractive in the first year?

calc.question: Calculate first-year profit after initial acquisition. Enter ₹ crore.
calc.working: Contribution ₹4.8 crore − fixed ₹3 crore − acquisition ₹1 crore = ₹0.8 crore.
calc.hint: Keep steady-state and first-year profit separate.

branches.shock: Paid pilot: 40% of the initial cohort leave after month 6; the rest stay 12 months. There are no replacements. Every active subscriber still orders 20 meals/month at ₹40 contribution. Fixed costs and initial acquisition cost remain unchanged.

stressCalc.question: Calculate first-year profit with this retention pattern. Enter ₹ crore.
stressCalc.working: 3,000×12 + 2,000×6 = 48,000 subscriber-months; ×20×₹40 = ₹3.84 crore; less ₹4 crore costs gives −₹0.16 crore.
stressCalc.hint: Count subscriber-months, not just year-end customers.

branches.probe: How would you measure retained cohorts without confusing discounts with product-market fit?
branches.model: The revised first year loses ₹0.16 crore. A small paid retention pilot or a deferred launch is defensible; require evidence on cohort retention and acquisition payback before scaling.

branches.title: Delivery density and scale
branches.focus: Investigate the subscriber threshold and route economics.
branches.evidence: Base economics remain ₹40 contribution/meal, 20 meals/month and ₹3 crore annual fixed costs. Assume full-year subscribers and exclude initial acquisition for the steady-state hurdle.
branches.question: What scale would meet the board’s profit hurdle, and can the operating model support it?

calc.question: Minimum whole subscribers needed for ₹1 crore annual operating profit?
calc.hint: The target profit is additional to fixed costs.

branches.shock: Route test: the planned rollout is entirely in dispersed areas, where delivered cost rises by ₹10/meal; price stays ₹150. The original variable cost was ₹110/meal. Current kitchen and delivery capacity is 5,000 full-year subscribers. Fixed costs stay ₹3 crore.

stressCalc.question: Minimum whole subscribers needed for the same ₹1 crore hurdle at the revised contribution?
stressCalc.working: Contribution falls to ₹30/meal; ₹4 crore/(₹30×240)=5,555.56, rounded up to 5,556. At capacity, profit is only ₹0.6 crore.
stressCalc.hint: Recalculate contribution before finding subscriber count.

branches.probe: Could a smaller, denser geographic launch beat a citywide launch? What must be validated?
branches.model: The threshold exceeds current capacity. Test a dense cluster, improve contribution or revise the plan; do not assume that adding dispersed customers will meet the profit hurdle.

strong: Separates survey intent, paid conversion and retention.
Differentiates first-year acquisition economics from steady-state profitability.
Links subscriber thresholds to achievable density and capacity.
pitfalls: Using year-end subscriber count for full-year revenue.
Treating stated intent as actual demand.
Ignoring the delivery-cost effect of geographic expansion.

clarifications: Are the rates nameplate or effective?
The initial line-capacity exhibit uses effective good-output rates, already including current losses.
Can the factory build inventory between stages?
Assume no buffer for the simplified line-capacity calculation. Real buffer design would require additional data.
What is the investment objective?
Supply 48,000 good packs/day reliably at minimal investment, without weakening quality.

extra.title: Product mix
extra.text: Demand varies across product formats. The current average rate does not prove capability for every shift and format.

extra.title: Rate measurement
extra.text: Use good packs after rejects when measuring effective rate. Avoid deducting the same loss twice.

branches.title: Reliability and product mix
branches.focus: Test whether the trial sustains customer demand.
branches.evidence: The improved packing trial suggests 6,200 good packs/hour. Mixing stays 7,000/hour and filling 8,000/hour. Demand is 48,000 good packs/day over 8 hours.
branches.question: How much operating cushion does the trial provide?

calc.question: What is the percentage capacity cushion above demand? Enter percent.
calc.hint: Compare spare daily capacity with demand.

branches.shock: Across production days, 60% of days run an easy format at 6,400 good packs/hour and 40% a difficult format at 5,200. These replace the initial 6,200 average. Every day is 8 hours; demand remains 48,000/day. Do not assume spare output can be carried to the next day.

stressCalc.question: What is average output across this mix of days?
stressCalc.working: (0.6×6,400 + 0.4×5,200)×8 = 47,360/day. Difficult-format days produce only 41,600. Demand is 48,000/day and spare output is not carried over, so on easy days output is capped by demand at 48,000: demand actually served averages 45,440/day (0.6×48,000 + 0.4×41,600), about 2,560/day goes unmet and full demand is met on 60% of days.
stressCalc.hint: Calculate the weighted average, then assess each day separately.

branches.probe: Why might an average be insufficient even if it met demand?
branches.model: The average misses demand and difficult-format days miss by 6,400 packs. Improve the difficult-format setup, validate shifts, or evaluate a temporary capacity option. Do not promise reliability from an average.

branches.title: Investment and payback
branches.focus: Compare inexpensive debottlenecking with a temporary alternative.
branches.evidence: Packing improvements cost ₹8 lakh upfront. Incremental contribution is ₹2 per extra good pack sold; only the additional 8,000 packs/day needed to meet demand can be sold. Assume 250 operating days/year and sustained production. A temporary packing contractor can instead supply the 8,000/day at an extra ₹0.80/pack relative to in-house variable cost, with no setup cost.
branches.question: What is the payback, and how would you compare a contractor during the trial?

calc.question: Simple payback for the ₹8 lakh packing improvement, in operating days?
calc.working: ₹800,000/(8,000×₹2)=50 operating days. Unsold excess capacity earns no contribution.
calc.hint: Use incremental sales, capped by demand.

branches.shock: A firm customer update reduces total demand to 44,000/day for all of the coming year. Baseline output stays 40,000/day; contribution remains ₹2/extra pack; investment remains ₹8 lakh. The six-month trial window contains 125 operating days.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate simple payback in operating days at the lower demand.
stressCalc.working: ₹800,000/(4,000×₹2)=100 operating days. This fits 125 days if the improvement is sustained.
stressCalc.hint: Only 4,000 extra packs can now be sold.

branches.probe: How does demand certainty affect committing capital versus using temporary capacity?
branches.model: The improvement still has 100 operating-day payback, but demand and execution must be validated. A contractor may bridge the trial; compare its incremental cost and quality before selecting it.

strong: Uses the system constraint, not the proposed equipment, as the starting point.
Does not double-count losses already embedded in effective rates.
Tests performance by format and caps benefits at sellable demand.
pitfalls: Improving filling without changing the bottleneck.
Converting all extra capacity into profit regardless of demand.
Relying on one average trial rate for service commitments.

clarifications: What is the target baseline?
Improve the current annual operating profit by at least ₹1 crore.
Are customer counts year-end figures?
Use full-year average customers unless a later scenario says otherwise.
Does service cost include fixed overhead?
₹300/customer/month is variable service cost; the ₹5 crore fixed cost is additional.

extra.title: Experiment design
extra.text: A test needs a control group, customer-level contribution, support effort and churn tracking. A short promotional response is not proof of a durable uplift.

branches.title: Broad price cut
branches.focus: Test contribution break-even and capacity.
branches.evidence: The proposal reduces monthly price from ₹1,000 to ₹850. Variable cost remains ₹300. Customer count rises from 10,000 to 12,500 for the full year. Fixed costs remain ₹5 crore.
branches.question: Does the sales projection actually improve profit?

calc.question: Calculate annual operating profit under the discount proposal. Enter ₹ crore.
calc.working: 12,500×(₹850−₹300)×12 − ₹5 crore = ₹3.25 crore. This is ₹0.15 crore below the baseline.
calc.hint: Compare contribution, not customer growth.

branches.shock: The paid test supports only 10% full-year average customer growth at the same discounted price. All other assumptions are unchanged.

stressCalc.question: Calculate annual operating profit at 11,000 customers. Enter ₹ crore.
stressCalc.hint: Use ₹550 monthly contribution.

branches.probe: What volume increase would merely preserve baseline profit? What about the ₹1 crore improvement target?
branches.model: Preserving ₹3.4 crore profit requires 12,728 whole customers, about 27.3% growth. Hitting ₹4.4 crore needs 14,243, beyond known support capacity. Reject a blanket cut or limit it to a controlled experiment.

branches.title: Segmented premium tier
branches.focus: Test monetisation of advanced users.
branches.evidence: All 7,000 standard users stay on ₹1,000/month with variable cost ₹300. Of the 3,000 advanced users, 70% adopt a ₹1,400 premium tier at variable cost ₹450; the rest retain the old plan. All remain for the full year. Additional annual product fixed cost is ₹30 lakh.
branches.question: How much incremental profit could a premium offer create?

calc.question: Calculate incremental annual operating profit versus the baseline. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.hint: Only migrating users create incremental contribution.

branches.shock: The pilot now indicates only 40% of advanced users will migrate; all others stay on the old plan. Costs are unchanged.

stressCalc.question: Calculate incremental annual operating profit with 40% migration. Enter ₹ lakh.
stressCalc.hint: Migration changes; total customers do not.

branches.probe: What additional benefit would be needed to meet the target? How could a smaller launch reduce fixed cost?
branches.model: A premium pilot remains slightly positive but cannot deliver the ₹1 crore target alone. Validate demand, limit development cost and investigate complementary retention or acquisition improvements.

strong: Calculates contribution effects instead of equating customer growth with profit.
Checks whether the hurdle requires capacity beyond what is known.
Separates migration from new customers and identifies fixed product cost.
pitfalls: Applying premium revenue to all users.
Ignoring service cost and capacity.
Presenting a small positive uplift as achievement of the full ₹1 crore target.

clarifications: What must improve?
Service as well as annual recurring savings. No single mandated on-time target has been agreed; propose a measurable one.
How do we treat inventory?
New inventory requires cash. Apply the specified annual carrying-cost rate in recurring economics, but discuss inventory cash separately from setup payback.
What is one-time payback?
For this exercise, setup expenditure divided by net recurring savings. This is not a full investment valuation.

extra.title: Order release
extra.text: Late release sometimes comes from inaccurate stock records and approval holds. A carrier contract alone will not remove those delays.

branches.title: Regional hub
branches.focus: Test network savings including inventory.
branches.evidence: Karnataka shipments would cost ₹130 each from the hub. Other regions stay unchanged. Annual hub fixed cost ₹18 lakh; additional average inventory ₹40 lakh with 20% annual carrying cost. Setup cost ₹20 lakh. All 30,000 Karnataka shipments use the hub in the initial scenario.
branches.question: Does the hub meet the saving and setup-payback requirements?

calc.question: Calculate net annual recurring savings from the hub. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.hint: Deduct fixed hub cost and inventory carrying cost.

branches.shock: A demand review reduces Karnataka shipments to 20,000/year. Other region volumes, unit freight saving, hub fixed cost, inventory and carrying rate remain unchanged. Compare the hub with serving this same lower volume from Chennai.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate net annual hub savings at the lower Karnataka volume. Enter ₹ lakh.
stressCalc.working: 20,000×₹170/100,000 − ₹18 lakh − ₹8 lakh = ₹8 lakh; setup payback 2.5 years.
stressCalc.hint: Compare two networks at the same volume.

branches.probe: What inventory and service evidence is needed before opening the hub?
branches.model: The hub passes the initial scenario but misses both economic hurdles at lower volume. A staged or smaller hub may be worth investigating, but do not invent lower costs; obtain a new quote and validate service.

branches.title: Carrier and warehouse release
branches.focus: Test a lower-capital service improvement.
branches.evidence: A carrier-and-cutoff programme saves ₹60/Karnataka shipment. It requires ₹5 lakh annual systems and coordination cost and ₹4 lakh one-time setup. Current Karnataka volume is 30,000/year. Other regions are unchanged.
branches.question: Can a process change meet the full savings objective, or only part of it?

calc.question: Calculate net annual recurring savings. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.working: 30,000×₹60/100,000 − ₹5 lakh = ₹13 lakh. Payback is 4/13 = 0.31 years, but savings miss the ₹20 lakh hurdle.
calc.hint: Separate setup from recurring cost.

branches.shock: A control-adjusted pilot shows only ₹35 saving per Karnataka shipment. Annual coordination cost remains ₹5 lakh, volume 30,000 and setup ₹4 lakh. Service improves from 78% to 90% on time in the pilot, but peak-season performance is untested.

stressCalc.question: Calculate revised recurring savings. Enter ₹ lakh.
stressCalc.working: 30,000×₹35/100,000 − ₹5 lakh = ₹5.5 lakh. Setup payback ≈0.73 years.
stressCalc.hint: Update only the verified unit saving.

branches.probe: Would you accept partial savings with improved service? What would you negotiate with the COO?
branches.model: A pilot can be justified for service and quick payback, but it does not meet the full saving target. Make the gap explicit and seek additional levers or revised scope before making a full commitment.

strong: Includes carrying cost and distinguishes cash tied in inventory from setup cost.
Compares alternatives at equal demand and uses net recurring savings.
Connects the service diagnosis to both carrier and internal-process changes.
pitfalls: Counting gross freight savings as net savings.
Ignoring inventory cash or treating inventory as an annual expense in full.
Meeting payback while silently dropping the annual savings target.

clarifications: What is an additional outcome?
A student who meets mastery because of the programme relative to their no-programme outcome. The arithmetic uses stated uplift assumptions; evidence must still establish causality.
Is equity a formal quota?
No quota is specified. Explain whose access is improved or worsened and what trade-off you propose.
How should uncertain data be used?
Show conditional calculations and design a credible evaluation. Do not present the voluntary pilot as causal evidence.

extra.title: Measurement plan
extra.text: Use a common pre/post assessment and comparison group; track attendance, attrition and outcomes by access group. Discuss fair allocation and informed participation with programme leaders.

branches.title: Digital engagement
branches.focus: Test the engagement assumption and delivery scale.
branches.evidence: A redesigned digital programme costs ₹12 lakh fixed + ₹400/enrolled student. It can reach 12,000 students with reliable access. Assume 90% engage; engaged learners gain 30 percentage points of mastery, non-engaged learners zero. There is no additional device budget.
branches.question: Can redesign meet the target, and who remains excluded?

calc.question: Calculate expected additional mastery outcomes.
calc.hint: Use enrolment × engagement × absolute uplift.

branches.shock: The wider trial finds engagement is only 65% at the same enrolment and assumed engaged-student uplift. Programme cost is unchanged. These observations do not yet resolve selection bias.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate expected additional mastery outcomes.
stressCalc.hint: Only engagement changes.

branches.probe: How would you distinguish ineffective teaching from poor access or engagement?
branches.model: The scaled scenario misses the target. Test engagement supports and causality before rollout; acknowledge the 8,000 students without reliable digital access. Do not claim the initial estimate as a verified impact.

branches.title: Community-supported learning
branches.focus: Compare access and impact under the same budget.
branches.evidence: Community learning costs ₹10 lakh fixed plus ₹1,000/enrolled student; enrol 5,000. Assume 95% engage and engaged students gain 50 percentage points of mastery. Non-engaged students have zero uplift. The eligible group has the same assumed 40% baseline, so a 50-point uplift is arithmetically feasible.
branches.question: How does this compare with the digital option on impact and inclusion?

calc.question: Calculate expected additional mastery outcomes.
calc.hint: A 50-percentage-point uplift is 0.50.

branches.shock: Facilitator constraints reduce feasible engagement to 80%, with the same enrolment, cost and uplift assumption. Community sites can include students without digital access.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate expected additional mastery outcomes.
stressCalc.hint: Count engagement explicitly.

branches.probe: What is a defensible recommendation if neither model meets the target?
branches.model: The supported model broadens access but misses the numeric target. Recommend a learning pilot or a mixed-design study, explicitly negotiate the target or budget and test outcomes with a credible comparison group.

strong: Separates percentage points from relative changes.
Distinguishes projected impact from causally demonstrated impact.
Discusses exclusion and recommends what to do when no scenario meets the target.
pitfalls: Counting every enrolled student as an incremental success.
Treating a selected voluntary pilot as a causal estimate.
Ignoring students without access because the digital unit cost is lower.

prompts.0: Define exactly what you are estimating. How would you break it into quantities you can reasonably approximate?
prompts.1: Build your assumptions before calculating. You may use the method notes, but requesting an exhibit is optional. Explain why your inputs are plausible.
prompts.3: Choose a numerical cross-check. Both routes use explicitly hypothetical inputs; compare their implications with your own first estimate.
prompts.5: Test the revised assumption. Recalculate the estimate and explain which uncertainty this resolves and which uncertainty remains.
prompts.6: State your final estimated range, its assumptions and the main uncertainty. Reconcile differences between methods without treating either as ground truth.
prompts.7: Which two data points would most improve the estimate? Describe how you would gather them and test for coverage or sampling bias.

guesstimate.assessmentInstruction: This is a guesstimate. Do not grade the initial estimate against a fixed reference total or penalise it for differing from the later hypothetical anchors. Assess scope, decomposition, explicit assumptions, order of magnitude, arithmetic, uncertainty and triangulation. No business solution or implementation recommendation is required.
clarifications: What is included?
Paid takeaway and delivered coffee cups within the stated boundary, including vendors; no home-made or dine-in coffee.
Can I choose my own assumptions?
Yes. The first estimate is open-ended and has no automatic right/wrong target. Later inputs are fixed hypothetical arithmetic exercises.
Should the final answer be exact?
No. Give a sensible range and identify what drives it; do not call a scenario range a statistical confidence interval.

branches.title: Demand-side cross-check
branches.focus: Use people, buying frequency and cup counts.
branches.evidence: For this checkpoint only, assume 8 million residents; 70% relevant adults; 40% of those adults buy coffee outside the home on a typical weekday; 25% of their outside-coffee purchases are takeaway; and 1.2 cups per buyer in the counted takeaway occasions. Treat these as independent multiplicative assumptions for the exercise. No additional tourist or commuter flow is included.
branches.question: Calculate this demand-side scenario and explain which assumptions you would challenge.

calc.question: Under these supplied assumptions, how many takeaway cups are sold per weekday?
calc.hint: Track the population base of each percentage.

branches.shock: The takeaway-share assumption is particularly uncertain: use 20% for a low scenario and 30% for a high scenario. Keep all other supplied inputs unchanged. This is a sensitivity range, not a measured confidence interval.

stressCalc.question: Calculate the LOW scenario in cups per weekday. Give the high scenario and interpretation in your explanation.
stressCalc.working: Low: 8m × .70 × .40 × .20 × 1.2 = 537,600. High at 30%: 806,400. This range varies only takeaway share, not all uncertainties.
stressCalc.hint: Change only the takeaway-share factor.

branches.probe: Which additional uncertainty could move the estimate outside this one-factor range?
branches.model: The supplied demand scenario gives roughly 0.54–0.81 million cups/day as takeaway share varies. Treat this as an illustrative sensitivity range, compare it with your own estimate and a seller-based check, and seek evidence on frequency and takeaway share before narrowing it.

branches.title: Supply-side cross-check
branches.focus: Count sellers and daily throughput without double-counting delivery.
branches.evidence: For this checkpoint only, assume 4,000 fixed outlets averaging 120 takeaway cups/day and 1,000 mobile sellers averaging 80/day. These categories do not overlap in the initial list. Delivered cups are already included in each seller’s count.
branches.question: Calculate the seller-based scenario and explain how you would check it independently.

calc.question: Under the supplied seller assumptions, estimate total cups per weekday.
calc.working: 4,000 × 120 + 1,000 × 80 = 560,000 cups/weekday. Do not add delivery cups a second time.
calc.hint: Sum the two seller categories.

branches.shock: A directory audit finds that 10% of the 4,000 fixed-outlet records are duplicate records, not additional sellers. Each remaining unique fixed outlet still averages 120 cups/day. Mobile seller count and throughput are unchanged.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate cups per weekday after removing duplicate fixed-outlet records.
stressCalc.working: 3,600 unique fixed outlets × 120 + 1,000 mobile sellers × 80 = 512,000 cups/day.
stressCalc.hint: Remove duplicate records before multiplying by throughput.

branches.probe: How would peak-hour observations and unequal outlet sizes bias an average-throughput estimate?
branches.model: The corrected seller scenario is about 0.51 million cups/day. Its precision is conditional on hypothetical throughput and complete seller coverage. Triangulate with the demand method and sample outlets by type and time of day; do not claim this as Chennai’s actual market size.

strong: Defines the market and units before estimating.
States defensible assumptions and checks double-counting and orders of magnitude.
Reconciles methods and explains the uncertainty rather than chasing a single target.
pitfalls: Counting customers as cups or adding delivery twice.
Using national or metropolitan population with municipal seller counts.
Presenting hypothetical anchors as measured Chennai data.

prompts.0: What is the symptom, and what would count as a well-supported diagnosis? Build competing explanations before choosing one.
prompts.1: Request evidence that can separate a real performance change from a measurement change. Explain what each observation supports or rules out.
prompts.3: Which diagnostic test would you prioritise: localising the affected cohort or reconciling independent records? Explain what the result would tell you.
prompts.5: New evidence challenges the headline story. Revise the diagnosis, distinguish facts from hypotheses and calculate the requested measure.
prompts.6: State the problem precisely: what changed, where, by how much and with what confidence? Separate proven observations from unproven causes. Do not recommend a fix.
prompts.7: Propose the next diagnostic tests, including the evidence that would confirm or falsify each remaining hypothesis. Do not design a solution or implementation programme.

diagnosis.assessmentInstruction: DIAGNOSIS-ONLY case. The candidate must identify and bound the problem, not recommend a solution. Do not ask for interventions, ROI of fixes or implementation. Do not penalise the absence of a solution. Evaluate symptom-versus-cause distinction, measurement validity, segmentation, competing hypotheses, causal caution and a falsifiable verification plan.
clarifications: Am I expected to solve the problem?
No. Your output is a quantified problem statement, a ranked set of explanations and the next evidence needed. Buying capacity or changing software is out of scope.
Can I trust the dashboard?
Treat it as a reported observation. Reconcile with independent source systems before concluding the whole decline is real.
Does the release prove causality?
No. Timing and concentration support investigation, but campaign mix and selection may confound the association.

branches.title: Localise the affected cohort
branches.focus: Compare platforms and versions before assigning a cause.
branches.evidence: Current Android checkout attempts are 60,000 and app-recorded confirmations 32,000. The previous Android recorded confirmation rate was 48,000/60,000 = 80%. iOS remains at 80%.
branches.question: Localise the recorded drop and distinguish an association from a root-cause claim.

calc.question: Calculate the current Android APP-RECORDED payment-confirmation rate. Enter percent.
calc.working: 32,000 / 60,000 × 100 = 53.33%, down 26.67 percentage points from 80%.
calc.hint: A percentage-point change differs from a relative percentage change.

branches.shock: Current Android cohort reconciliation: old-version users made 15,000 attempts with 12,000 confirmations in both app and bank records. New-version users made 45,000 attempts: the app recorded 20,000 confirmations, while the bank verifies 28,000 paid transactions. Thus 8,000 new-version payments are missing from app confirmation records. iOS bank confirmations remain 32,000. No independent shipment audit is available on this path.

stressCalc.question: What is the BANK-VERIFIED payment-success rate for the new-version Android cohort? Enter percent.
stressCalc.working: 28,000 / 45,000 × 100 = 62.22%. App-recorded rate was 44.44%. Total bank payments are 12,000 + 28,000 + 32,000 = 72,000 versus 80,000 previously.
stressCalc.hint: Use the independent bank numerator for the specified cohort.

branches.probe: What could explain the cohort difference besides a software defect, and what would falsify that explanation?
branches.model: The new Android cohort has both under-recording and a lower bank-verified payment-success rate. Of the 16,000 apparent payment-confirmation loss, 8,000 is an app-recording gap; bank payments are down 8,000 overall. Version association is not causal proof. Reconcile shipment outcomes and compare like-for-like cohorts or a controlled rollout before asserting the exact order impact or root cause.

branches.title: Reconcile independent records
branches.focus: Separate reporting error from the underlying operational change.
branches.evidence: The bank independently verifies 80,000 paid transactions in the prior week and 72,000 in the current week. The app recorded 80,000 and 64,000 payment confirmations respectively. IDs and time windows have been reconciled; duplicates and refunds are excluded consistently.
branches.question: How much of the apparent payment-confirmation decline is a recording gap?

calc.question: How many current-week bank-verified paid transactions are missing from app confirmation records?
calc.working: 72,000 bank-verified payments − 64,000 app confirmations = 8,000 missing app confirmations.
calc.hint: Compare the two sources in the same week.

branches.shock: An independent shipment audit now verifies 50,000 completed orders previously and 45,000 currently, versus 40,000 currently in the app dashboard. Bank-paid transactions are 80,000 and 72,000. The bank-to-shipment conversion is therefore unchanged at 62.5%. The discrepancy is concentrated on Android, but no controlled evidence yet establishes the mechanism.

stressCalc.question: What is the VERIFIED decline in completed orders, as a percentage of the previous week?
stressCalc.working: (50,000 − 45,000)/50,000 × 100 = 10%. The other 5,000 orders in the apparent 10,000 decline are a reporting gap.
stressCalc.hint: Use shipment-audited orders, not dashboard counts.

branches.probe: Which transaction-level joins or controlled comparisons would distinguish a gateway fault, app fault and customer-mix change?
branches.model: The apparent 20% order decline combines a verified 10% decline and a 5,000-order reporting gap. Bank payments also declined 10%, while verified downstream conversion is stable. Prioritise diagnosing payment-stage loss and the measurement discrepancy, especially on Android; do not claim a delivery shortage or a proven software root cause. Specify transaction reconciliation and controlled cohort tests next.

strong: Distinguishes the reported symptom from independently verified performance.
Quantifies where the loss occurs and maintains multiple causal explanations.
Ends with a precise problem statement and tests that could falsify the leading hypothesis, without jumping to an intervention.
pitfalls: Taking the dashboard at face value.
Calling the release a proven cause merely because it occurred at the same time.
Recommending more delivery capacity before localising the loss.

investment.assessmentInstruction: Strategic investment case. Compare cash flow, NPV, service feasibility and strategic trade-offs. Use the supplied annuity factor. Accept build, partner, pilot or defer decisions when supported; do not favour a single answer merely because base-case NPV is higher.
clarifications: Which financial measure should I use?
NPV at 10% over five years. Simple payback may supplement the analysis but is not the decision criterion.
Are depreciation and tax included?
No. Work directly with the supplied operating cash flows and time-zero outlay; do not add tax shields or residual value.
Does positive NPV imply approval?
No. Demand and the 98% service target must also be supported. You can recommend a conditional decision or defer commitment.

branches.title: Owned facility downside
branches.focus: Test capital commitment and an overrun.
branches.evidence: Use annual operating cash flow of ₹60 lakh for five years, upfront investment ₹200 lakh and annuity factor 3.791. No terminal value. For comparison, the partner’s annual cash flow at base volume is 70,000×₹60/100,000 − ₹8 lakh = ₹34 lakh, with ₹20 lakh upfront cost.
branches.question: Is ownership attractive in absolute terms and compared with the partner?

calc.question: Calculate the owned facility’s base-case NPV. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.hint: Subtract upfront investment after discounting annual cash flows.

branches.shock: A binding construction quote raises owned-facility upfront investment from ₹200 lakh to ₹250 lakh. Annual operating cash flow remains ₹60 lakh. The partner base economics are unchanged. There is no quantified strategic premium that offsets the overrun.

stressCalc.question: Calculate revised owned-facility NPV after the capital overrun. Enter ₹ lakh.
stressCalc.hint: Only time-zero capital cost changes.

branches.probe: What evidence might justify ownership despite a worse financial case, and how would you avoid inventing that value?
branches.model: Ownership now has negative NPV under the stated economics. A conditional partner arrangement or deferral is more defensible unless a redesigned cost structure or evidenced strategic benefit changes the case. Validate demand and service before treating the partner’s higher NPV as sufficient.

branches.title: Partner performance downside
branches.focus: Test lower realised volume and contract risk.
branches.evidence: Partner base annual cash flow is ₹34 lakh and upfront integration ₹20 lakh. Use five years and factor 3.791. The owned base NPV is ₹27.46 lakh under its original ₹200 lakh investment.
branches.question: How attractive is the partner option, and what operational risks could overturn that conclusion?

calc.question: Calculate partner base-case NPV. Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.hint: Use net contribution after partner charges, not customer revenue.

branches.shock: A pilot suggests the partner can support only 60,000 pallet-months/year. Net contribution stays ₹60/pallet-month, annual contract-management cost stays ₹8 lakh, and additional expected annual service credits payable by ColdLink are ₹6 lakh. Upfront cost remains ₹20 lakh. These replace the partner base assumptions for all five years. The pilot achieves 96% service, below the board’s 98% target.

stressCalc.question: Calculate partner NPV under the revised volume and service-credit assumptions. Enter ₹ lakh.
stressCalc.hint: Deduct the recurring service credits before discounting.

branches.probe: Would you approve a positive-NPV contract that fails the service requirement? What would your decision depend on?
branches.model: The revised partner NPV remains positive at ₹63.402 lakh, but the pilot fails the 98% service target. Require a credible service remedy and retest economics, evaluate another partner, or defer. Do not approve unconditionally on NPV alone or assume service can be fixed at zero cost.

strong: Uses incremental cash flows and consistent timing for both alternatives.
Updates NPV for the changed assumption and separates financial attractiveness from service feasibility.
Discusses strategic control, dependence and reversibility without inventing quantified benefits.
pitfalls: Subtracting capital expenditure from every annual cash flow.
Comparing accounting profit with discounted cash flow.
Ignoring the service hurdle because NPV is positive.

prompts.0: Orders fell about 13% week on week. Before guessing causes, what would you clarify about the metric and the timing, and how would you break the problem down?
prompts.1: Which data would you look at first to separate internal causes from external ones? Request exhibits and state your leading hypothesis, and what would rule it out.
prompts.3: Two cuts look promising: split the payment step by platform and app version, or check the drop against payment-gateway records first. Which would you do first, and what would each result tell you?
prompts.5: New data has arrived. How does it change your explanation? Recalculate and say what you would now tell leadership.
prompts.6: Explain what happened, how confident you are, and what the team should do this week. Separate the action from what still needs verifying.
prompts.7: How would you know the fix worked? Name the metric, a guardrail, the comparison you would use and when you would check.

metricdrop.assessmentInstruction: Product analytics root-cause case. Assess metric definition, funnel decomposition, segmentation, sizing the impact, separating correlation from cause, and a proportionate action with a measurement plan. Accept a rollback, a paused rollout or a targeted fix when the evidence supports it.
metricdrop.closingNote: Lead with what happened and how sure you are. Separate the action for this week from what still needs to be verified.
clarifications: How is an order counted?
An order is counted when payment succeeds. Cash on delivery is not offered. Cancellations are tracked separately and did not change.
Did anything else change around 3 March?
Prices, delivery fees and marketing spend were unchanged. Product releases and other context are in the exhibits.
What does leadership need?
A clear explanation, how confident you are, and an action for this week. A permanent fix can come later.

branches.title: Split by platform and version
branches.focus: Find which users the payment drop affects.
branches.evidence: Latest week, checkouts started and payments succeeded. Android 8.2: 1,75,000 checkouts, 87,500 payments. Android 8.1 (not updated): 1,75,000 checkouts, 1,40,000 payments. iOS: 1,50,000 checkouts, 1,20,000 payments. In the prior week every group converted at 80%.
branches.question: What does the breakdown tell you, and how big is the problem?

calc.question: How many weekly orders did Android 8.2 lose, assuming its users would otherwise have converted at the same 80% as everyone else? Enter orders.
calc.working: Android 8.2 converted at 87,500 ÷ 1,75,000 = 50%. Expected at 80%: 1,40,000. Lost: 1,40,000 − 87,500 = 52,500 orders, the whole fall from 4,00,000 to 3,47,500.
calc.hint: Compare actual payments with what 80% conversion would have produced for the same checkouts.

branches.shock: Engineering finds that Android 8.2 fails only on phones with less than 3 GB of memory: the new checkout page crashes when the UPI app hands back. Those phones are 60% of Android 8.2 checkouts, and payment success on them is 30%. On other 8.2 phones it is 80%. A rollback to 8.1 can ship in 2 days; a proper fix needs 10 days.
