stressCalc.question: Android 8.2 has about 25,000 checkouts a day. If you roll back in 2 days instead of waiting 10 days for the fix, how many orders do you save over those 8 days? Assume the rollback restores 80% success. Enter orders.
stressCalc.working: Affected checkouts: 25,000 × 60% = 15,000 a day. Lost per day: 15,000 × (80% − 30%) = 7,500 orders. Over 8 days: 7,500 × 8 = 60,000 orders.
stressCalc.hint: Only the low-memory phones are affected. Work out orders lost per day, then multiply by the days saved.

branches.probe: What would you check before rolling back, so you do not throw away what 8.2 does well?
branches.model: The drop is a payment failure on Android 8.2, concentrated on low-memory phones, and it explains all 52,500 lost weekly orders. Roll back for affected phones now: that saves about 60,000 orders compared with waiting for the 10-day fix. Then ship the fix through a staged rollout guarded by crash rate and payment success, and confirm recovery to about 4,00,000 orders a week against users who stayed on 8.1.

branches.title: Check the payment records
branches.focus: Confirm the drop is real and find where in payment it happens.
branches.evidence: The payment gateway settled 3,47,200 transactions in the latest week; the app recorded 3,47,500, a normal gap from refund timing. Dark stores packed 3,47,100 orders. Payment attempts that did not succeed: 1,00,000 in the prior week and 1,52,500 in the latest week. Gateway error codes are unchanged; the extra failures show as “user did not return from UPI app”.
branches.question: Is the drop real, and where in the payment step is it happening?

calc.question: By what percentage did failed payment attempts rise week on week? Enter %.
calc.working: (1,52,500 − 1,00,000) ÷ 1,00,000 = 52.5% more failed payments. The gateway and dark-store counts match the app, so this is a real drop, not a tracking error.
calc.hint: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old.

branches.shock: Failures split by app version: Android 8.2 had 1,75,000 checkouts and 87,500 failed payments. All other users had 3,25,000 checkouts and 65,000 failures, the same 20% failure rate as the prior week.

stressCalc.question: How many more failed payments did Android 8.2 have than the normal 20% failure rate would produce? Enter failed payments.
stressCalc.working: Expected failures at 20%: 1,75,000 × 20% = 35,000. Actual: 87,500. Extra: 87,500 − 35,000 = 52,500, which matches the whole fall in orders.
stressCalc.hint: Compare actual failures with what the normal rate predicts for the same checkouts.

branches.probe: The release passed QA. What would you change so a problem like this is caught before it reaches half of Android users?
branches.model: The drop is real: gateway and dark-store records agree with the app. It sits entirely at the payment step, with about 52,500 extra failures, all from Android 8.2 users not returning from their UPI app. Pause the 8.2 rollout or roll back now, reproduce the UPI hand-back on real devices, and resume only through a staged rollout guarded by payment success. Still unknown: which phones are affected, and whether the new checkout page or saved UPI causes it.

strong: Clarifies how the metric is counted and checks the drop against normal variation before hunting for causes.
Uses the funnel to find the step where the drop happens, then segments that step to find who is affected.
Separates the urgent action from verifying the cause, and says how recovery will be measured.
pitfalls: Listing every possible cause (competitors, weather, pricing) without using the data to narrow down.
Blaming the release only because of the timing, without checking that unaffected users stayed normal.
Recommending a fix with no way to measure whether orders recovered.

prompts.0: What is the streak meant to achieve for learners and for the business? Before looking at results, what would success look like, and what could go wrong?
prompts.1: Choose a primary metric and a few guardrail metrics. Request the experiment data you need and explain why each metric matters.
prompts.3: Before you trust the result, which would you check first: whether the effect lasts, or whether the experiment itself is sound? Explain what each check could reveal.
prompts.5: New evidence has arrived. How does it change your reading of the experiment? Recalculate and say what you now believe.
prompts.6: Should PadhoPlus launch the streak to everyone, launch a changed version, or keep testing? Give your decision, the numbers behind it and the main risk.
prompts.7: How would you roll it out or test it next? Name the decision metric, the guardrails that would make you stop, and when you would review.

experiment.assessmentInstruction: Product metrics and experimentation case. Assess metric choice tied to the goal, guardrails, correct reading of absolute versus relative lift, checks on durability and experiment validity, and a decision proportionate to the evidence. Do not require a formal significance test; the brief says the result is significant. Accept launch, redesign or further testing when justified.
experiment.closingNote: Tie the decision to the primary metric and the guardrails. Say what result would change your mind.
clarifications: What is the company goal?
More paid subscribers this year. Retention is a leading indicator, but leadership will not trade real learning for app opens.
Was the primary metric chosen before the test?
Yes. Week-4 retention was written down as the primary metric before the test started.
Do I need to test statistical significance?
No. The data team confirms the week-4 difference is statistically significant at this sample size. Focus on what the result means.

branches.title: Does the effect last?
branches.focus: Look at retention over time and the quality of practice.
branches.evidence: Retention by week, control vs streak: week 1, 30% vs 36%; week 2, 24% vs 27.6%; week 3, 20% vs 21.6%; week 4, 18.0% vs 19.8%. Among learners still active in week 4, 40% of streak learners did only 1-minute quick reviews, against 15% in control.
branches.question: Is the streak building a learning habit, or just more app opens?

calc.question: How many extra learners out of 40,000 are still active in week 4 because of the streak? Enter learners.
calc.working: 40,000 × (19.8% − 18.0%) = 40,000 × 1.8% = 720 extra learners. The relative lift shrinks from 20% in week 1 to 10% in week 4.
calc.hint: Multiply the group size by the percentage-point difference.

branches.shock: Week-8 retention has now come in: control 14.0%, streak 14.7%. Streak learners’ quiz scores are still 8 points lower, and their notification opt-outs have risen to 7%.

stressCalc.question: What is the relative lift in week-8 retention? Enter %.
stressCalc.working: (14.7% − 14.0%) ÷ 14.0% = 0.7 ÷ 14 = 5%. The week-8 lift is half the week-4 lift and well below week 1 (20%, 15%, 8% and 10% in weeks 1 to 4). It has not fallen steadily (week 4 was above week 3), so ask what explains the uneven pattern.
stressCalc.hint: Divide the difference by the control rate.

branches.probe: If the lift keeps shrinking, what would you need to see before launching?
branches.model: The streak raises early engagement, but the retention lift fades (10% relative at week 4, 5% at week 8) and learning quality falls: more 1-minute reviews, lower quiz scores and rising opt-outs. Do not launch it as it is. Test a redesigned streak that counts only full lessons, with quiz score and notification opt-outs as guardrails and week-8 retention as the decision metric.

branches.title: Is the experiment sound?
branches.focus: Check who was really exposed and what the metric means.
branches.evidence: The split was 40,000 and 40,000, as planned. But 4,000 learners in the streak group were on an old app version and never saw the streak. They are still counted in the streak group, and they retained like control, at 18.0% in week 4.
branches.question: Can you trust the 10% lift, and what does it mean for learners who actually saw the streak?

calc.question: What is week-4 retention among the 36,000 streak-group learners who actually saw the feature? Enter %.
calc.working: Streak group active in week 4: 40,000 × 19.8% = 7,920. Unexposed learners active: 4,000 × 18.0% = 720. Exposed learners active: 7,920 − 720 = 7,200. 7,200 ÷ 36,000 = 20%. This assumes the 4,000 unexposed learners retained at the control rate; exposure depended on app version, so it is an estimate, not a randomised comparison.
calc.hint: Work in numbers of learners, not percentages: remove the unexposed learners from both the top and the bottom.

branches.shock: Trial-to-paid conversion at day 14 is now in: control 6.0% of sign-ups, streak 5.7%. Each paid subscriber is worth ₹2,000 in their first year.

stressCalc.question: What is the change in first-year subscription revenue per 40,000 sign-ups if the streak launches? Enter ₹ lakh, negative if it falls.
stressCalc.hint: Turn both conversion rates into subscribers first, then multiply the difference by the value per subscriber.

branches.probe: Retention went up but paid conversion went down. How would you explain that to leadership, and what would you test next?
branches.model: The randomised result is 19.8% against 18.0% (+1.8 percentage points). Learners who actually saw the streak retained at about 20%, but that is an estimate that rests on assuming the 4,000 unexposed learners retained at the control rate. Exposure depended on app version, so a fair check would compare learners on app versions that could show the streak in both groups. Observed paid conversion was lower (5.7% against 6.0%), about ₹2.4 lakh less first-year revenue per 40,000 sign-ups as a point estimate. With 40,000 sign-ups in each group, a gap that size is within what chance alone could produce (roughly −0.63 to +0.03 percentage points at 95%), so it is a risk to check rather than an established fall. Do not launch to everyone yet. Find out whether conversion really fell and, if so, why, such as weaker learning or reminder fatigue, and test a revised streak with paid conversion as a guardrail.

strong: Defines success by the company goal and names guardrail metrics before reading the results.
Separates absolute and relative lift, and turns rates into numbers of learners or rupees.
Checks whether the effect lasts and whether the experiment is sound before recommending a launch.
pitfalls: Declaring success because week-1 retention rose 20%, ignoring the week-4 metric chosen in advance.
Ignoring guardrails (quiz scores, opt-outs, paid conversion) that moved the wrong way.
Mixing up percentage points with percentage change.

prompts.0: Who are KiranaPay’s users, and what do they need from the app? What would you clarify before comparing the three ideas?
prompts.1: Which user problems matter most, and for whom? Request the research and data you need, and say which segment you would focus on.
prompts.3: There are two ways to compare the ideas: score them on reach, impact, confidence and effort, or estimate what each could earn. Which would you lead with, and why?
prompts.5: A new constraint has come up. How does it change your ranking? Recalculate and explain what you would now build.
prompts.6: Which feature should KiranaPay build first? Give the user problem it solves, the numbers behind your choice, the main risk, and what you are choosing not to build.
prompts.7: How would you test the feature before a full launch? Describe the first version, who gets it, the success metric, the guardrails and the result that would make you stop.

prioritise.assessmentInstruction: Product sense and prioritisation case. Assess user segmentation, problem selection grounded in the research, opportunity sizing, explicit trade-offs, sensitivity to uncertain inputs, and a testable first version. Accept any well-supported feature choice, including switching after the new constraint.
prioritise.closingNote: Name the user problem first, then the feature. Be explicit about what you are choosing not to build, and why.
clarifications: What is the company goal this year?
Grow the payment value processed and reduce shopkeeper churn. Revenue matters, but leadership will accept a feature that mainly protects retention.
Can we build more than one feature?
Only one major feature this quarter. Small experiments, such as a survey, a landing page or a manual pilot, can run alongside it.
Can I make assumptions about what shopkeepers want?
Yes, but ground them in the research and data in the exhibits, and say how you would check them.

branches.title: Score the ideas (RICE)
branches.focus: Compare reach, impact, confidence and effort.
branches.evidence: RICE score = reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort in months. Reach is shopkeepers likely to use the feature in a quarter. Instant settlement: reach 18,000, impact 2, confidence 80%, effort 2. Stock tracker: reach 30,000, impact 1, confidence 50%, effort 4. Loans: reach 6,000, impact 3, confidence 50%, effort 5.
branches.question: How do the three ideas compare, and how far do you trust the scores?

calc.question: What is the RICE score for instant settlement? Enter the score.
calc.hint: Multiply reach, impact and confidence (as a decimal), then divide by effort.

branches.shock: The bank partner says instant settlement now needs a new compliance review: effort rises from 2 to 4 months and the team’s confidence falls to 60%. Separately, the stock-tracker team finds a ready-made item catalogue, cutting its effort to 2 months.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate the RICE score for instant settlement. Enter the score.
stressCalc.working: 18,000 × 2 × 0.6 ÷ 4 = 5,400. Stock tracker is now 30,000 × 1 × 0.5 ÷ 2 = 7,500, so it ranks first. Loans stay at 1,800.
stressCalc.hint: Change only the effort and confidence for settlement.

branches.probe: The scores now favour the stock tracker. Would you switch? What would you check about the scores first?
branches.model: On the original scores instant settlement leads clearly (14,400 against 3,750 and 1,800), and it matches the most raised problem for larger stores. After the compliance delay it falls to 5,400, below the stock tracker at 7,500. RICE is only as good as its inputs: the tracker’s 50% confidence is a guess and its impact is unproven. A strong answer either runs a quick stock-tracker test while settlement clears compliance, or keeps settlement first because it solves the top researched problem for the most valuable stores, and explains the trade-off.

branches.title: Estimate the revenue
branches.focus: Compare what each idea could earn in its first year.
branches.evidence: Year-one estimates. Instant settlement: ₹162 lakh a month at 30% adoption among larger stores, but with the ramp-up there are about 6 full months of revenue in year one. Loans: 6,000 loans in the year, averaging ₹25,000, with KiranaPay keeping 2%. Stock tracker: free, so no direct revenue; the team hopes it cuts monthly churn for the 30,000 small stores using it from 4% to 3%.
branches.question: Which idea creates the most value, and is revenue the right way to compare them?

calc.question: What is year-one revenue from instant settlement? Enter ₹ lakh.
calc.working: ₹162 lakh × 6 months = ₹972 lakh, about ₹9.7 crore. Loans: 6,000 × ₹25,000 × 2% = ₹30 lakh. The stock tracker earns nothing directly.
calc.hint: Use the 6 months of revenue, not 12.

branches.shock: Rival app PayDukaan has just launched free instant settlement. To stay competitive KiranaPay would have to cut its fee from 0.3% to 0.1%, with adoption still expected at 30% of larger stores. Without instant settlement, the team expects larger-store churn to rise from 2% to 4% a month.

stressCalc.question: Recalculate year-one revenue from instant settlement at a 0.1% fee. Enter ₹ lakh.
stressCalc.working: Revenue scales with the fee: ₹972 lakh × (0.1% ÷ 0.3%) = ₹324 lakh. Or: ₹540 crore × 0.1% = ₹54 lakh a month × 6 months = ₹324 lakh.
stressCalc.hint: Only the fee changes; adoption and volume stay the same.

branches.probe: If a rival gives it away free, is instant settlement still a growth feature, or has it become something every app must have? How does that change your recommendation?
branches.model: At a 0.3% fee instant settlement earns about ₹972 lakh in year one, far more than loans (₹30 lakh) and the stock tracker (no direct revenue). After the rival’s move it earns ₹324 lakh at 0.1%, but its main value is now defensive: without it, larger stores, who carry about two-thirds of payment value, may leave at twice the rate. Build instant settlement first. A 0.1% fee narrows the gap with the rival’s free offer without matching it, so check whether stores still adopt at a fee, and judge it on larger-store churn as well as revenue. Revisit loans once settlement data shows which stores have steady cash flow.

strong: Segments the users and ties the choice to a specific problem from the research.
Sizes the opportunity and the effort, and says which uncertain inputs could change the ranking.
Proposes a small first version with a success metric, guardrails and a condition for stopping.
pitfalls: Choosing the most exciting idea (loans) without weighing effort, regulation or which users asked for it.
Treating a RICE score as a precise answer instead of a rough comparison built on guesses.
Recommending a full launch with no test, metric or stop condition.
